newsitem.title: USA: Deadly Empire State shooting seen as random attack.
newsitem.headline: Deadly Empire State shooting seen as random attack.

text.p: U.S. authorities were reviewing security at the Empire State Building on Monday after a shooting spree by an elderly Palestinian but officials said it appeared to be a random attack without political motivation.

The gunman, identified as 69-year-old Palestinian Ali Abu Kamal, killed a young rock musician from Denmark on Sunday and wounded six other people before taking his own life with a gun he bought legally in Florida.
The tragedy also prompted politicians and gun control advocates bitterly decried the ease with which a foreign visitor to the United States could purchase a powerful gun.
"We have no reason to believe that this was someone other than a deranged individual acting on his own," New York City Police Commissioner Howard Safir told a news conference.

The widow of the alleged gunman said in an interview in Gaza on Monday that her husband was not politically motivated but in despair over having been cheated out of $500,000. She said her husband had travelled to the United States last December seeking a financier for a new investment company.
"My husband is not a terrorist, he was just hopeless," Fathiya Abu Kamal, 55, said. "He was aged, he had nothing to do with politics, or terrorism, or crime."
Empire State Building owners were meeting on Monday to review security at the landmark, which does not have metal detectors.

Mayor Rudolph Giuliani told reporters that building staff were being trained to use metal detectors and that the observation deck would be closed to visitors all day Monday, reopening on Tuesday morning.

A building security camera tape that shows the gunman on the way up to the observation deck was given to police, Empire State building spokesman Howard Rubenstein said. "He was wearing a long coat. The gun was not visible and presumably it was hidden under his coat," Rubenstein said.

The gunman shot dead 27-year-old Christoffer Burmeister, jazz guitarist for the Bush Pilots rock band, and wounded six other people -- Matthew Gross, 29, of Connecticut who played in the same band, a 52-year-old Argentine man, a 30-year-old Swiss man, a 35-year old Bronx, N.Y. man and a married couple from Verdun, France.
Police said the gunman died without regaining consciousness in a New York hospital about six hours after he shot the tourists and then turned the gun on himself.
Three of the wounded were in critical condition on Monday and three others were serious but stable, hospital officials said.

Officials said the gunman was carrying documents from the Palestinian Authority that showed he lived in Ramallah on the West Bank and was born in Jaffa. He came to New York in December and legally bought the .380-calibre Beretta that he used in the shooting in Florida at the end of January.

New York Democratic Congresswoman Carolyn McCarthy, who became a gun control lobbyist after her husband was shot dead and her son wounded on a commuter train in 1993, told reporters that national gun laws had to be changed.
"The time has come, it's an embarassment to this country," McCarthy told reporters.
Several other people were injured in the pandemonium that broke out after the shooting on the 86th floor observation deck, which was crowded with tourists on a sunny on Sunday afternoon.
The attack was the worst bloodshed at the 102-story building since July 1945, when a B-25 bomber lost in fog crashed into the 79th floor, killing 14 people and injuring 26 others.
